titleStmt.title: Fighting COVID-19 Misinformation on Social Media: Experimental Evidence for a Scalable Accuracy-Nudge Intervention
titleStmt.author: Gordon Pennycook
Jonathon McPhetres
Yunhao Zhang
Jackson G. Lu

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Fighting COVID-19 Misinformation on Social Media: Experimental Evidence for a Scalable Accuracy-Nudge Intervention

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: why people share false claims they could have identified as false, and whether the gap can be closed by making accuracy salient
span.quote: A key outcome from the news task is truth discernment—that is, the extent to which individuals distinguish between true and false content in their judgments. Discernment is defined as the difference in accuracy judgments (or sharing intentions) between true and false headlines. For example, an individual who shared 9 out of 15 true headlines and 12 out of 15 false headlines would have a discernment level of −.2 (i.e., .6 – .8), whereas an individual who shared 9 out of 15 true headlines and 3 out of 15 false headlines would have a discernment level of .4 (i.e., .6 – .2). Thus, a higher discernment score indicates a higher sensitivity to truth relative to falsity.

span.label: whether the inattention account of political fake-news sharing extends to COVID-19 misinformation, where the content is largely apolitical and the stakes are life and death
span.quote: It was unclear, however, how (or whether) these results would generalize to COVID-19. First, it may be that a greater level of specialized knowledge is required to correctly judge the accuracy of health information relative to political information. Thus, participants may be unable to discern truth from falsehood in the context of COVID-19, even when they do consider accuracy.

span.label: a measured dissociation between accuracy judgment and sharing intention on the same headlines, and a randomised test showing that one accuracy judgement about an unrelated headline raises sharing discernment 2.8-fold
span.quote: As predicted, we observed a significant positive interaction between headline veracity and treatment, β = 0.039, F(1, 25623) = 17.88, p < .0001; the treatment increased sharing discernment (i.e., participants were more likely to share true headlines relative to false headlines after they rated the accuracy of a single non-COVID-related headline; Fig. 2). Specifically, although participants in the control condition were not significantly more likely to say that they would share true headlines compared with false headlines, d = 0.050, 95% CI = [−0.033, 0.133], F(1, 25623) = 1.41, p = .24, in the treatment condition, sharing intentions for true headlines were significantly higher than for false headlines, d = 0.142, 95% CI = [0.049, 0.235], F(1, 25623) = 8.89, p = .003. Quantitatively, sharing discernment (the difference in sharing likelihood of true relative to false headlines) was 2.8 times higher in the treatment condition compared with the control condition.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Theoretically, our findings shed new light on the perspective that inattention plays an important role in the sharing of misinformation online. By demonstrating the role of inattention in the context of COVID-19 misinformation (rather than politics), our results suggest that partisanship is not, apparently, the key factor distracting people from considering accuracy on social media. Instead, the tendency to be distracted from accuracy on social media seems more general.

span.label: truth discernment that is present when people are asked about accuracy and nearly absent when the same people are asked what they would share
span.quote: We began by comparing discernment—the difference between responses to true headlines and false headlines—across conditions. As predicted, we observed a significant interaction between headline veracity and condition, β = −0.126, F(1, 25586) = 42.24, p < .0001, indicating that discernment was higher for accuracy judgments than sharing intentions (Fig. 1; similar results were obtained when we excluded the few headlines that did not contain clear claims of fact or that were political in nature; see Table S3 in the Supplemental Material). In other words, veracity had a much bigger impact on accuracy judgments, Cohen’s d = 0.657, 95% confidence interval (CI) = [0.477, 0.836], F(1, 25586) = 42.24, p < .0001, than on sharing intentions, d = 0.121, 95% CI = [0.030, 0.212], F(1, 25586) = 6.74, p = .009.

span.label: two preregistered survey experiments on quota-matched US samples, 853 and 856 participants, 15 true and 15 false COVID-19 headlines in Facebook-post format, analysed at the rating level with standard errors clustered on participant and headline
span.term: two preregistered survey experiments on quota-matched US samples, 853 and 856 participants, 15 true and 15 false COVID-19 headlines in Facebook-post format, analysed at the rating level with standard errors clustered on participant and headline
span.quote: Lucid uses quota sampling to provide a sample that is matched to the U.S. public on age, gender, ethnicity, and geographic region. We selected Lucid because it provides a sample that is reasonably representative of the U.S. population while being affordable for large samples.

span.label: the account is not that people want to spread falsehood, nor that they cannot tell the difference. It is that the sharing context puts other things in front of accuracy - social approval, partisan alignment, the fact that news sits between baby photos - so the preference exists and is simply not applied at the moment of decision
span.term: a preference that is never consulted
span.quote: According to this account, people generally wish to avoid spreading misinformation and, in fact, are often able to tell truth from falsehood; however, they nonetheless share false and misleading content because the social media context focuses their attention on factors other than accuracy (e.g., partisan alignment). As a result, they get distracted from even considering accuracy when deciding whether to share news—leading them to not implement their preference for accuracy and instead share misleading content.

span.label: the treatment is one accuracy judgement about a politically neutral headline unrelated to the topic, framed as a pretest. It supplies no information about COVID-19 and no instruction about sharing; what it does is raise the accessibility of the concept of accuracy, and the effect is a change in what the participant attends to rather than in what they know
span.term: a prime that carries no content
span.quote: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the control condition, they began the news-sharing task as in Study 1. In the treatment condition, they rated the accuracy of a single headline (unrelated to COVID-19) before beginning the news-sharing task; following, we framed this as being for a pretest. Each participant saw one of four possible headlines, all politically neutral and unrelated to COVID-19 (see https://osf.io/7d3xh/ for materials). An advantage of this design is that the manipulation is subtle and not explicitly linked to the main task. Thus, it is unlikely that any between-conditions difference was driven by participants’ believing that the accuracy question at the beginning of the treatment condition was designed to make them take accuracy into account when making sharing decisions during the main experiment. It is therefore relatively unlikely that any treatment effect was due to demand characteristics or social desirability.

span.label: if the nudge works by directing attention to accuracy, then its effect on a headline should track how accurate that headline is perceived to be - pushing sharing up for the clearly true and down for the clearly false. Measured across the thirty items using Study 1's ratings as the accuracy scale, r(28) = .76
span.term: the item-level signature of an attention effect
span.quote: As shown in Figure 3, there was indeed a strong positive correlation between a headline’s perceived accuracy and the impact of the treatment, r(28) = .76, p < .0001. Headlines that were more likely to be identified as true (on the basis of Study 1 data) were more strongly positively impacted (sharing increases) by nudging people to consider accuracy. This suggests that the accuracy nudge, as we hypothesized, increased people’s attention to whether the headlines seem true or not when they decided what to share.

span.label: the evidence is restricted to the United States, and the sample is quota matched rather than probability sampled so it is not nationally representative
span.quote: Our research has several limitations. First, our evidence is restricted to the United States and therefore needs to be tested elsewhere in the world. Next, although our sample was quota matched to the U.S. population on age, gender, ethnicity, and region, it was not obtained via probability sampling and therefore should not be considered truly nationally representative.

span.label: one particular set of thirty headlines was used, and misinformation in other forms - e-mails, text posts, memes - is untested
span.quote: We also used a particular set of true and false headlines about COVID-19. It is important for future work to test the generalizability of our findings to other headlines and to information (and misinformation) about COVID-19 that comes in forms other than headlines (e.g., e-mails, text posts, and memes about supposed disease cures).

span.label: sharing intentions were hypothetical and the induction was performed in a lab context, so extension to naturalistic social media is an inference
span.quote: Finally, our sharing intentions were hypothetical, and our experimental accuracy induction was performed in a “lab” context. Thus, one may be concerned about whether our results will extend to naturalistic social media contexts.

span.label: accuracy nudges are described by the authors as far from a complete solution
span.quote: Although accuracy nudges are far from a complete solution, the intervention may nonetheless have important downstream effects on the overall quality of information shared online (e.g., because of network effects; see). Furthermore, our treatment translates directly into a suite of real-world interventions that social media companies could easily deploy by periodically asking users to rate the accuracy of randomly sampled headlines.

span.label: one false headline turned out on inspection to be misleading or unverified rather than untrue, and was retained after checking that removing it changed nothing
span.quote: After the study was completed, we realized that one of the false headlines (about bats being the source of the virus) was more misleading or unverified than untrue—however, removing this headline did not change our results, and so we retained it.

span.label: the preregistration specified clustering standard errors on participant only, and the published analysis clusters on participant and headline
span.quote: Our preregistration erroneously indicated that we would cluster standard errors only on participant; doing so does not qualitatively change the results.

span.label: priming - raising the accessibility of a concept with an unrelated task - carried from cognitive psychology into a platform-deployable intervention against misinformation
span.quote: Prior to deciding which headlines they would share on social media, participants were subtly primed to think about accuracy by being asked to rate the accuracy of a single non-COVID-related news headline. This minimal, content-neutral intervention nearly tripled participants’ level of discernment between sharing true and sharing false headlines.

span.label: the nudge frame from behavioural economics: change what is salient at the moment of choice rather than what the chooser knows or is allowed to do
span.quote: Such interventions are easily scalable and do not require platforms to make decision about what content to censor.

span.label: the accuracy induction disguised as a pretest, using a single politically neutral headline unrelated to the topic of the sharing task
span.note: eliminates: demand characteristics and social desirability as the explanation of the treatment effect - a participant who cannot see what the manipulation is for cannot comply with it · outcome: held
span.quote: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the control condition, they began the news-sharing task as in Study 1. span.label: apolitical COVID-19 content used in place of the political headlines the prior literature used, with partisanship measured and tested as a moderator
span.note: eliminates: partisan motivation as the thing distracting people from accuracy - the effect survives when the content gives partisanship nothing to work with · outcome: held
span.quote: Furthermore, the treatment effect on sharing discernment was not significantly moderated by CRT performance, science knowledge, partisanship, distance to the nearest epicenter, or MMS score (ps >.10 for all three-way interactions among headline veracity, treatment, and individual-differences measure). The treatment effect was also robust to excluding the few headlines that did not contain clear claims of fact or that were political in nature (see Table S6 in the Supplemental Material).

span.label: a post hoc item-level analysis correlating each headline's treatment effect against its perceived accuracy from the other study's participants
span.note: eliminates: a general suppression of sharing as the explanation - an attention effect must push true headlines UP and false ones down, and the correlation is r(28) = .76 · outcome: held

span.label: all participants retained in the main analyses regardless of failing the three attention screeners, per the preregistered plan, with the key result reported across levels of attentiveness
span.note: eliminates: the effect being an artefact of who was excluded - dropping inattentive respondents would trade representativeness for a cleaner sample and the authors show the result does not depend on the trade · outcome: held
span.quote: To maintain the representativeness of our sample, we followed our preregistered plan to include all participants in our main analyses, regardless of attentiveness. As can be seen in Table S2 in the Supplemental Material available online, our key result was robust (the effect size for the interaction between content type and condition remained consistent) across levels of attentiveness.

span.label: one false headline reclassified after data collection as misleading rather than untrue, and the analysis rerun without it
span.note: eliminates: a defective stimulus carrying the result - the item is disclosed, the removal is tested, and it is retained on the strength of the test rather than quietly · outcome: held
span.quote: After the study was completed, we realized that one of the false headlines (about bats being the source of the virus) was more misleading or unverified than untrue—however, removing this headline did not change our results, and so we retained it.

span.label: linear probability models used for interpretability, with logistic regression run alongside
span.note: eliminates: the functional form as the source of the result - the readable model and the conventional one are reported to agree · outcome: held
span.quote: Our main analyses used linear probability models instead of logistic regression because the coefficients are more readily interpretable. However, logistic regression yielded qualitatively equivalent results.

span.label: the self-reported sharing measure checked against a headline-level relationship between reported willingness and actual shares on Twitter
span.note: eliminates: a hypothetical intention being read as behaviour with no evidence at all - the link is external and at the level of the item · outcome: partial
span.quote: the validity of this self-report sharing measure is evidenced by the observation that news headlines that Mechanical Turk participants report a higher likelihood of sharing indeed receive more shares on Twitter.

span.label: results also reported excluding the few headlines that were political or that did not contain a clear claim of fact
span.note: eliminates: a handful of atypical items driving the interaction · outcome: held

span.label: a preregistration deviation declared in the paper - the plan specified clustering on participant only - with the preregistered version run

span.label: three screener questions embedding a subtle instruction inside a block of text, placed before each of the main tasks
span.note: eliminates: participants who click through without reading - on a task about whether people can tell true headlines from false ones · outcome: held
span.quote: Following the recommendations of, we added three screener questions that put a subtle instruction in the middle of a block of text. For example, in a block of text ostensibly about which news sources people prefer, we asked participants to select two specific options (“FoxNews.com” and “NBC.com”) to check whether they were reading the text.

span.label: a leave-one-out check on the stimulus set: one false headline judged after the fact to be misleading rather than untrue was removed and the analysis re-run
span.note: eliminates: that the result rests on one badly-classified item - the paper re-ran without it, found no change, and retained it while saying so · outcome: held
span.quote: Through a partnership with Harvard Global Health Institute, we acquired a list of 15 false and 15 true news headlines relating to COVID-19 (available at https://osf.io/7d3xh/). The false headlines were deemed to be false by authoritative sources (e.g., fact-checking sites such as snopes.com and factcheck.org, health experts such as mayoclinic.com, and credible science websites such as www.livescience.com). After the study was completed, we realized that one of the false headlines (about bats being the source of the virus) was more misleading or unverified than untrue—however, removing this headline did not change our results, and so we retained it. The true headlines came from reliable mainstream media sources.

span.quote: A key outcome from the news task is truth discernment—that is, the extent to which individuals distinguish between true and false content in their judgments. Discernment is defined as the difference in accuracy judgments (or sharing intentions) between true and false headlines. span.label: accuracy nudge
span.quote: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the control condition, they began the news-sharing task as in Study 1. In the treatment condition, they rated the accuracy of a single headline (unrelated to COVID-19) before beginning the news-sharing task; following, we framed this as being for a pretest. Each participant saw one of four possible headlines, all politically neutral and unrelated to COVID-19 (see https://osf.io/7d3xh/ for materials). An advantage of this design is that the manipulation is subtle and not explicitly linked to the main task. Thus, it is unlikely that any between-conditions difference was driven by participants’ believing that the accuracy question at the beginning of the treatment condition was designed to make them take accuracy into account when making sharing decisions during the main experiment. It is therefore relatively unlikely that any treatment effect was due to demand characteristics or social desirability.

span.label: CRT
span.quote: We found that scores on the CRT were positively related to both accuracy discernment and sharing discernment, as revealed by the interactions between CRT score and veracity, F(1, 25582) = 34.95, p < .0001, and F(1, 25582) = 4.98, p = .026, respectively. However, the relationship was significantly stronger for accuracy, as indicated by the three-way interaction among CRT score, veracity, and condition, F(1, 25582) = 14.68, p = .0001. In particular, CRT score was negatively correlated with belief in false headlines and uncorrelated with belief in true headlines, whereas CRT score was negatively correlated with sharing of both types of headlines (albeit more negatively correlated with sharing of false headlines compared with true headlines; for effect sizes, see Table 1). The pattern of CRT correlations observed here for COVID-19 misinformation is therefore consistent with what has been seen previously with political headlines.

span.quote: Furthermore, the treatment effect on sharing discernment was not significantly moderated by CRT performance, science knowledge, partisanship, distance to the nearest epicenter, or MMS score (ps >.10 for all three-way interactions among headline veracity, treatment, and individual-differences measure). span.quote: As shown in Figure 3, there was indeed a strong positive correlation between a headline’s perceived accuracy and the impact of the treatment, r(28) = .76, p < .0001. Headlines that were more likely to be identified as true (on the basis of Study 1 data) were more strongly positively impacted (sharing increases) by nudging people to consider accuracy. This suggests that the accuracy nudge, as we hypothesized, increased people’s attention to whether the headlines seem true or not when they decided what to share.

span.quote: A key outcome from the news task is truth discernment—that is, the extent to which individuals distinguish between true and false content in their judgments. Discernment is defined as the difference in accuracy judgments (or sharing intentions) between true and false headlines. For example, an individual who shared 9 out of 15 true headlines and 12 out of 15 false headlines would have a discernment level of −.2 (i.e., .6 – .8), whereas an individual who shared 9 out of 15 true headlines and 3 out of 15 false headlines would have a discernment level of .4 (i.e., .6 – .2). Thus, a higher discernment score indicates a higher sensitivity to truth relative to falsity.
